Mysuru.name: Mysuru
Mysuru.tagline: Mysore or Mysuru is the second-largest city of the Indian state of Karnataka after Bengaluru.

info.intro: Mysore or Mysuru is the second-largest city of the Indian state of Karnataka after Bengaluru. It was the capital of the Wodeyar dynasty and is considered to be the cultural capital of Karnataka. Mysore is among the cleanest and best-planned cities in India. The regal city is striking a balance between olden times and modernity, resulting in the city being both old and new.
info.understand: Name and history Mysore's recorded history dates back over a thousand years. Its name has a mythological origin. According to Hindu mythology, the demon Mahishasura was slain by the Goddess Chamundi at the place where present-day Mysore is. A statue of Mahishasura stands on Chamundi Hill on the outskirts of the city. In later times, the city rose to prominence when it became the capital of a breakaway vassal state of the Vijayanagara Empire, ruled by the Wodeyar family in 1584. In 1610, the king Chamaraja Wodeyar shifted the capital to nearby Srirangapatna. Hyder Ali, who was a commander in the army, usurped power in the late 18th century. Hyder Ali was succeeded by his son Tipu Sultan, who fought and lost a war with the British, dying in battle in 1799. The British restored the Wodeyars as their puppet rulers and shifted the capital back to Mysore.
info.get_in: The nearest international airport is in Bengaluru, 185 km northeast. is the city's main station, and daily trains are plying the route to Bengaluru. Mysore is well connected to Bengaluru, with about 18 pairs of trains plying between them daily. Express Trains like 12007/08 Chennai Shatabdi, 16231/32 Mayiladuthurai Express (via Trichy), 16215/16 Chamundi Express, 16235/36 Tuticorin Express (via Madurai), 16021/22 Chennai Kaveri Express, 16591/92 Hampi Express, 16219/20 Tirupati Express, 16535/36 Gol Gumbaz Express (via Hubli, Bagalakot), 16557/58 Rajya Rani Express, 17307/08 Basava Express (via Kalaburagi, Solapur), 12613/14 Wodeyar Express, 16023/24 Malgudi Express, 17325/26 Vishwamanava Express (Hubli), 16227/28 Talaguppa Express and 3 sets of passenger trains connect Bengaluru to Mysuru daily.
info.get_around: Getting around in Mysore is cheaper than in most Indian cities. By thumb Taking a lift, most of the locals (mainly 2-wheelers) are very helpful and generally stop to give a lift. It might be difficult on the main arterial roads because of the Traffic Police, as helmets are compulsory for pillion riders as well. By bus City buses originate from the City Bus Stand, 2 km from the Railway Station. Frequent bus services are available to all major city tourist and residential areas. Bus stops and departure times are visible on online map services. Volvo air-conditioned buses are available to Chamundi Hills, KRS-Brindavan Garden, Zoo, Infosys, and the European Quarter (Gokula). By car Tourist cabs are your best option if you plan to tour the city all day or go to neighbouring towns like Srirangapatna. Costs about ₹9 or ₹10 per km.
info.stay_safe: Mysore is regarded as a safe and peaceful city. However, if you plan to wander around during the night, it is suggested that you be watchful, as a few incidents of purse and chain snatching are reported every once in awhile. It is good idea to be alert if you are using an autorickshaw during when it is late, especially if you are alone. Also be careful when paying money to the autorickshaw drivers since they may tout non-locals, and can overcharge and decline using the meter at certain places and times. Note that hire taxi services are another option in Mysore. The police in Mysore are helpful and friendly. Do not hesitate to request for assistance. You can reach the police control room by dialling 108 from a mobile phone or alternatively, 100 from a landline. The people of Mysore are by and large peace-loving and hospitable.

attraction.name: Mysore Zoo
attraction.area: Sri Chamarajendra Zoological Gardens, Zoo Main Road Indiranagar
attraction.text: The zoo was established under royal patronage in 1892, making it one of the oldest in the world. Mysore Zoo has had a successful breeding program and houses animals from more than 40 different countries, along with native Indian fauna, including Royal Bengal tigers, white tigers, elephants, fallow deer, Himalayan...
attraction.price: ₹40 for adults, ₹10 for children over 5, battery operated vehicle tour ₹100,...

attraction.name: Mysore Palace
attraction.text: Definitely the number one attraction in Mysore. Intricately carved rosewood doors and ceilings, some with inlaid ivory work, marble figurines, collections of caskets, paintings of the members of the royal family and other objects of personal use exhibit such opulence, and over time have been preserved remarkably well.
attraction.price: ₹100 for both Indian and foreign adults

attraction.name: Jayalakshmi Vilas
attraction.text: It was built by Maharani Regent Vani Vilasa Sannidhana, wife of Chamaraja Wodeyar, for her daughter Jayalakshami. It has around 200 rooms, an exotic dancing hall and a Kalyanmantap with intricately carved wood pillars.

attraction.name: Lalitha Mahal Palace
attraction.text: Another palace that has been turned into a five-star hotel. It served as a royal summer residence for the Viceroy of India in the late 19th and early 19th century. You feel the antique-style grandeur and regality when you stay here.

attraction.name: Chamundeshwari Temple
attraction.text: A beautiful temple of Goddess Chamundeshwari (or Chamundi Devi) with marvellous architecture. Wheelchair access is available. AC Volvo buses go up to Chamundi Hill and back from the city bus stand every twenty minutes.

attraction.name: Folklore Museum
attraction.text: Founded in 1968 and located in the University of Mysore campus, the museum has over 6500 folk art and folklore articles on display and exhibits arts and crafts from all over the state of Karnataka. It is housed in Jayalakhmi Mansion situated at Manasa Gangotri.

attraction.name: Jaganmohan Palace and Art Gallery
attraction.area: opposite City Bus Stand, Jagan Mohan Palace Road, Chamrajpura
attraction.text: A former palace that has been converted into an art gallery and function hall. The palace for some time was home to the Wodeyar dynasty. The art gallery features paintings of many styles, including Mughlai, Mysorean and European. The most prominent works are those of Raja Ravi Varma, which are over 100 years old.
attraction.image: A side wide angle view of Jaganmohan Palace, Mysuru, Karnataka.jpg

attraction.name: Kalashree Seashell Museum
attraction.text: A museum with sculptures made of seashell and conch by Radha Mallappa, including the sculptures of Ganesha, Shiva, the Taj Mahal and St. Philomena's Church.

attraction.name: Mysore Sand Sculpture Museum
attraction.text: 150 sand sculptures on display. It is not worth visiting unless it is on your way to another location.

attraction.name: Railway Museum
attraction.area: near the back gate of the railway station
attraction.text: Exhibits vintage locomotives as they were in use. The second of such museums was set up after the Rail Museum in Delhi. The major attraction of the museum is the wagon used by the Queen of Mysore. There is a small toy train.

attraction.name: Regional Museum of Natural History
attraction.area: near Nandhini Milk Dairy, back side of Postal Training Centre
attraction.text: Has exhibits on plants, animals, and geology of the southern region of India. They conduct a show at intervals. They also have a cute watch tower for bird watching. The museum is situated in a beautiful garden. You can even visit the place just sit to in the gardens in the lush green surroundings.

attraction.wiki: Regional Museum of Natural History Mysore

attraction.name: Sri Venugopala Swamy Temple
attraction.text: The Venugopala Swamy Temple is an example of Hoysala architecture. It was built in the 12th century around the same time as the Chennakesava Temple at Somanathapura. It is surrounded by water, a pleasant sight.

restaurant.name: Sambhrama Restaurant
restaurant.text: Good place for dosa, uppittu and other snacks. Their Akkirotti is a specialty.

restaurant.name: Aramana Restaurant
restaurant.text: Good quality vegetarian food and good ambience.

restaurant.name: Suvarna Shanthi Sagar
restaurant.text: Vegetarian lunch 12:30PM to 3PM, vegetarian dinner 7PM to 11:45PM.

restaurant.name: Green Leaf

restaurant.name: Hotel Mylari

restaurant.text: Good hall with a view upstairs.

restaurant.name: Hotel Nalapak
restaurant.text: Multi-cuisine restaurant which specialises in South Indian food.

restaurant.name: Pepe's
restaurant.text: Pure vegetarian restaurant serving South and North Indian, as well as some Indo-Chinese.

restaurant.name: The Sixth Main
restaurant.text: Small in size with a casual dining vibe but has a good vibe. Popular among both foreigners and Indians. Serves decent Thalis and Indo-Chinese.

restaurant.name: Suvarana Bhavan Vegetarian

restaurant.name: Ashirwad Restaurant
restaurant.text: Fine idlis and dosa varieties. Plain breakfast comes to around ₹100 per person.

restaurant.name: Bisibele Baath
restaurant.text: Made of rice and lentils with a lot of local spices. This is one of the most sought after dishes of Mysore. It is served hot and usually costs ₹25 in an average restaurant.

photo.text: Not to be confused with the one in Bengaluru, this one is cleaner.

photo.text: The perimeter is 3.6 km. There are many birds to see and the footpath is well maintained with small gardens around it.

photo.text: Have a nice walk on the embankment of Lingambudhi Lake. It will refresh you beyond description. This is a one-hour walk and ends up in Lingam Budhi village near the ring road. The famous University Layout is a residential suburb of this area.

photo.name: Lookout View Point
photo.text: The lookout provides an aerial view of Mysore, allowing you to see the entire white city and surrounding forest in all its glory. There are a few binoculars at the lookout point, though you would need to pay to use them.

photo.name: Karanji Lake
photo.text: A small lake inside the city. This is a favourite spot for romantic couples. You can go for a small trip of boating. The lake is surrounded by green trees and you can also see the various variety of birds like pelicans and painted storks on the island in Karanji Kere.

photo.name: University Lake
photo.text: Visitors can take a pleasant morning or evening stroll at the University Lake, Kukkarahalli. The perimeter is 3 km long.

Delhi.name: Delhi
Delhi.tagline: Delhi, the largest city in northern India, is the country's thriving melting pot.

info.intro: Delhi, the largest city in northern India, is the country's thriving melting pot. It contains New Delhi, the capital of modern India, as well as the capitals of several empires. Straddling the holy Yamuna River, Delhi is the centre of education, politics and transport in India, and the core of the National Capital Region (NCR). The city has a population of over 20 million in 2024. Delhi contains a striking array of historic sites for tourists to visit, as well as a nearly unlimited choice of shopping, food, museums, entertainment and nightlife.
info.understand: Travellers with little experience of visiting developing megacities may find Delhi to be chaotic at its worst, crowded and for much of the year, polluted. Air pollution has been a major problem in Delhi since the 1980s, with much of the day dominated with a very unhealthy amount of particles. During the late spring and early summer months, the city is scorchingly hot. Dig a little deeper, however, and you will get a glimpse of order beneath the chaos, as well as India's traditional and modern cultural richness flourishing side by side. First-time visitors experiencing culture shock are advised not to compound it by visiting during adverse weather conditions and get a decent hotel room so you can stay in comfort between your sightseeing trips. In addition, read up on the various scams and other uncomfortable situations travellers to India often encounter.
info.get_in: By bus Buses arrive from Kathmandu and Chitwan in Nepal (36 hr+) and virtually every city in India. Although not as comfortable as the trains, buses are the only choice for some destinations, mainly those in the mountains. Delhi has three major Inter-State Bus Terminals (ISBTs): Kashmere Gate, Sarai Kale Khan and Anand Vihar. The Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) is the major operator, but every state also runs its own buses and there are some private operators too. Once you have purchased a ticket either at the ticket office or on-line prior to the trip, all you need to do is go to the rail car labelled with your class of service purchased. You can either get on and sit in the first available seat or, for higher classes of service, they will often post a passenger list on the car when it stops. Look for your name and go to the assigned car, cabin and seat.
info.get_around: Getting around Delhi is always an adventure. Traffic is, by and large, horribly congested and many drivers will think nothing of quoting ten times the going price to a tourist. Use the prices below as broad guidelines and agree on prices before setting off. The best way to travel is via metro, where there are separate cabins for women (which prove to be very useful during rush hour). Metro is clean, efficient, and typically ridden by relatively affluent middle-class students or commuters en route to/from work; there is almost nowhere in the city that you cannot get to by metro. The massive Delhi Metro network provides a cheap, quick, mostly hassle-free and air-conditioned way of zipping around the city, although its increasing popularity means that rush hour crowds at key interchanges are starting to resemble Mumbai.
info.stay_safe: In an emergency, dial. The number connects to police, fire, ambulance, women and child helplines. The Delhi Police (DP) is responsible for law enforcement in the whole city. Police vehicles (called PCR vans) are parked on almost every major intersection. In addition, the Delhi Metro is patrolled by the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF). On the whole, Delhi is a marginally safe place to visit, especially for male travellers. However, it can be more dangerous than other parts of India, especially for women. Many first-time travellers to India find themselves falling victim to scams and touts, and unfortunately Delhi has a lot of both. Be on guard for anybody trying to help you by giving you unsolicited directions or travel advice. Do not blindly rely on the advice of taxi and auto drivers.

attraction.name: Jhandewalan Mandir
attraction.area: Jhandewalan Devi Mandir Marg, Block E, Jhandewalan Extension,...
attraction.text: One of the most popular temples of goddess Durga.

attraction.name: Akshardham
attraction.text: Completed in 2005 by the socio-spiritual organisation BAPS, no expense has been spared in decorating this large and elaborate temple carved of red sandstone. The central monument, built without any steel, houses an 11-ft golden statue of the founder of the Swaminarayan faith, Bhagwan Swaminarayan.
attraction.price: Free entry, guide booklet is ₹5, access to multimedia exhibitions ₹125

attraction.name: Red Fort
attraction.text: One of Delhi's top tourist sights and listed as a. A brilliant red sandstone fort was built by the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan (who also built the Taj Mahal) as his ruling palace.

attraction.name: Chhatta Chowk
attraction.text: True to the name, this is a covered bazaar between the gate and the fort itself, now filled with souvenir hawkers.

attraction.name: Diwan-i-Am
attraction.text: This building separates the outer court from the inner court and has a marble platform for the emperor's throne.

attraction.name: Diwan-i-Khas
attraction.text: Built completely of marble, this is where the emperor received special visitors.

attraction.name: Hayat Bakhsh Bagh
attraction.text: Once a grand garden full of fountains and streams, now sadly all dry, only dry channels and acres of green grass remain. Near here will you find the Sawan Pavilion.

attraction.name: Khas Mahal
attraction.text: The emperor's main residence. The octagonal Mussaman Burj tower looks out toward the Yamuna River and is where the Emperor used to appear before the public each morning.

attraction.name: Mumtaz Mahal
attraction.text: Contained six apartments for emperor's harem. Now used as a museum of court textiles, carpets, weapons, etc.

attraction.name: Rang Mahal
attraction.text: The residence of the emperor's main wife.

attraction.name: Salimgarh Fort
attraction.text: A fort built in 1546 by Salim Shah Suri, the son of Sher Shah Suri. At the time, the Mughal Empire had been temporarily overthrown, as Sher Shah Suri defeated Mughal emperor Humayun and established the rule of the Sur Empire rule in Delhi.

attraction.name: Delhi Town Hall
attraction.text: It was the seat of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) from 1866 till late 2009, when offices shifted to a new building at Minto Road. There used to be a clock tower near the town hall till the 1950s when it was demolished.

restaurant.name: Karim's
restaurant.text: Jama Masjid, Gali Kababian. As you'd expect from a restaurant on Kebab Lane, the main dish is Mughal-style meat (mutton and chicken), served up since 1913. Is down a little alley just South of the Jama Masjid southern entrance (past the auto supplies market).
restaurant.price: Under ₹200 at the original; more at the branches

restaurant.name: Gung The Palace
restaurant.text: A very up-market place with good food. 1st floor features a live karaoke, but the ground floor is the place to be. Book in advance for the ground floor.

restaurant.name: La Piazza
restaurant.area: Hyatt Regency, Ring Rd, Bhikaji Cama Place, Rama Krishna Puram
restaurant.text: Italian style restaurant.

restaurant.name: The Lazeez Hotel And Restaurant
restaurant.area: 87, New, Block I, Lajpat Nagar II, Lajpat Nagar
restaurant.text: Owned &amp: run by members of the Afghani community settled in the area.

restaurant.name: Side Wok
restaurant.text: Japanese, Chinese and other Asian food. Some choice of sushi. Beautiful decor. No alcohol.

restaurant.name: Haldiram's
restaurant.area: 1454/2 Chandni Chowk just west of the fountain and other outlets...
restaurant.text: This is a famous manufacturer of Indian snacks and sweets that has now gone global. This always-packed, two-story outlet in the heart of Chandni Chowk was its first in Delhi and dates back to 1924.

restaurant.name: Kake Di Hatti
restaurant.text: Kake Di Hatti has a variety of naans along with North Indian curry vegetables, like Dal Makhani, Shahi Paneer etc. The naans are very big and usually one naan is enough for two people.
restaurant.price: One person can eat within ₹200 to ₹250

restaurant.name: Pandit ji parathe wale
restaurant.text: established over 140 years ago,offers paratha, an Indian stuffed bread in Chandni Chowk.

restaurant.name: Ghantewala
restaurant.text: a sweet shop established in 1790, serves delicious delights and offers wide range of sweets.

cafe.name: Tadka 4986
cafe.area: Ram Dwara Rd, Nehru Bazar, Paharganj
cafe.text: A notably clean restaurant by Paharganj standards. Serves only vegetarian food, a full thali for ₹ 60. Their tea is really good and their most popular dish is paneer masala.

cafe.name: T.L.R. Cafe & Kitchen
cafe.area: 2nd Floor, 31, Hauz Khas Village, Near Axis Bank ATM New Delhi
cafe.text: Popular among tourists, expats and locals. Continental menu featuring a variety of pastas and panini sauce. Kitchen open 11AM-11PM daily. Also Spanish, Moroccan and American styles, plus desserts and drinks.

cafe.name: Amici Cafe
cafe.text: Italian style restaurant.

cafe.name: The Big Chill
cafe.text: Khan Market and East of Kailash, is popular with a young crowd for great smoothies, ice creams, cheesecakes and Italian food. Expect a waiting line during lunch at Saturdays.

cafe.name: Aap ki Pasand
cafe.area: Sterling House, 15 Netaji Subhash Marg, Daryaganj
cafe.text: Tea Shop, A great place to sample Indian chai and the exotic Darjeeling and Assam teas and buy tea in handcrafted fabric bags. Located in an old colonial era building, its teas have been savored by Bill Clinton, Gorbachov, Koizumi and are taken as official state gifts of India.

cafe.name: ''Old kheer shop
cafe.text: chawri bazaar, Chandni Chowk offers the famous Indian dessert named kheer'' with great legacy taste, established in 1880,over 140 years ago.

cafe.name: ''Old famous jalebi wala
cafe.text: '', offers an Indian dessert named jalebi in Chandni Chowk, established over 100 years ago.

cafe.name: ''Old ameer mithai wala
cafe.text: '', near Jama Masjid is another banger sweet and dessert shop that offers wide range of menu options including spicy grilled Indian sandwich called samosa and pakora, established over 100 years ago.

photo.name: Hayat Bakhsh Bagh
photo.text: Once a grand garden full of fountains and streams, now sadly all dry, only dry channels and acres of green grass remain. Near here will you find the Sawan Pavilion.

photo.name: Raj Ghat
photo.text: The memorial to Mahatma Gandhi at the site of his cremation. Check for closure dates/security checks around national holidays/Gandhi's death anniversary.

photo.name: Kisan Ghat
photo.text: The memorial to Charan Singh, the fifth Prime Minister of India.

photo.name: National Gandhi Museum
photo.text: The museum was first opened in Mumbai, shortly after Gandhi was assassinated in 1948. It was later moved to Raj Ghat in 1961. The library at the Gandhi Museum not only showcases Gandhi's work to the public but also serves as a place for general study.

photo.name: Tilpath Valley Biodiversity Park
photo.text: A biodiversity park northwest of Asola Bhatti Wildlife Sanctuary. It was developed by the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) from 2015 to 2018.

photo.name: Sanjay Lake Park
photo.area: Gate no 3 Sanjay Lake, Mayur Vihar
photo.text: A newly built adventure park comprising a range of outdoor activities, from water sports and treetop courses to archery and beach volleyball. The adventure park also has an artificial lake which attracts migratory birds and is surrounded by indigenous trees.

photo.name: Garden of Five Senses
photo.text: Partly built over a rocky terrain, the garden has various theme areas, including a section on the lines of Mughal Gardens, plus pools of water lilies, bamboo courts, herb gardens and a solar energy park.

photo.name: Yamuna Ghat
photo.text: Enjoy the scene of ritual bathing and sunset on the Yamuna River, which is considered sacred to Hindus along with the Ganges.

photo.name: Vijay Ghat
photo.text: The memorial to Lal Bahadur Shastri, the second Prime Minister of India.

Mumbai.name: Mumbai
Mumbai.tagline: Mumbai, formerly known as Bombay, is the largest city in western India and the capital of the state of Maharashtra.

info.intro: Mumbai, formerly known as Bombay, is the largest city in western India and the capital of the state of Maharashtra. A cosmopolitan metropolis, Mumbai was built on seven islands on the Konkan coastline which over time were joined to form the island city of Bombay. The island was in turn joined with the neighbouring island of Salsette to form "Greater Bombay". The city has a metropolitan population of over 20 million (2025). Often called the "New York of India", Mumbai is undoubtedly the country's commercial capital and one of the predominant port cities.
info.understand: Mumbai (MOOM-bigh) is a bustling, diverse metropolis with a flair of its own. The entrepreneurial spirit and pulsing pace of life provide a sharp contrast to much of the rest of India. Name There has been much debate regarding the original name of the city. Some say the current name of the city Mumbai is the original name; and is an eponym derived from Mumbā, a local Hindu goddess, and āī, meaning "mother" in Marathi. Others claim Bombay was an anglicised version of Bom Bahia, a name given by the Portuguese to mean "Beautiful Bay" and later made popular by the British as the name of the Bombay state. The name was officially changed from Bombay to Mumbai in 1995. Although both names are common, people who explicitly use "Bombay" are generally non-Marathi speakers, whereas "Mumbai" proponents primarily speak Marathi.
info.get_in: Mumbai has excellent connectivity with most of the major cities around the world, including New York, London, Dubai, Singapore, Hong Kong and Kuala Lumpur to name a few. If you are flying from Europe it is generally cheaper to fly from London, and there are many frequent flights available. All domestic sectors are linked to Mumbai, making it the second busiest hub in the country next to Delhi. By boat Thane Creek is bustling with ferries to central Mumbai from various cities on the southern and eastern side of the creek, such as Alibag. Ferries from Ferry Wharf also allow cheap access to islands and beaches in the vicinity of the city and Elephanta. There are no scheduled international ferries to Mumbai, however cruise ships dock regularly. Hundreds of trains arrive daily from all over India, almost all major cities have a direct connection with Mumbai.
info.get_around: Most of Mumbai's inhabitants rely on public transport to and from their workplaces due to the lack of parking spaces, traffic bottlenecks and generally poor road conditions, especially in the monsoon. However, do ride in a taxi at least once in the city. Feel real adventure in a vehicle that feels like it might fall apart at speed with a driver who thinks he's Schumacher. For travelling using public transport, you can download the m-Indicator app for Android and iPhone. It contains useful information about bus and train routes, which can help you plan your commute. The Mumbai Suburban Railway, commonly referred to as "Locals", is both an icon and a vital artery of Mumbai and a ride on it should be on every visitor's agenda. There are three primary lines in the city center — the Western Line, the Central Line and the Harbour Line.
info.stay_safe: Mumbai is considered one of India's safer major cities, with low rates of violent crime against foreigners. Opportunistic crimes like pickpocketing, bag snatching, and phone theft in crowded areas, are more common. The southwest monsoon season affecting Mumbai can make travel difficult from the airports due to rains and flooding which is possible. Red alerts issued by the Indian Meteorological Service are common during the monsoon and cloudbursts are uncommon here. Take extra care during travel during the rainy season. Here are a few basic safety tips: Always carry some cash as many places won't take cards. However, do not openly display ₹500 notes in public. The available notes are ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200 and ₹500 and the available coins are ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 and ₹20.

attraction.name: Gateway of India
attraction.text: The landmark gateway was built in 1911 to commemorate the visit of King George V and Queen Mary to India. Built in the Indo-Saracenic style, the foundation stone for the Gateway of India was laid on 31 March 1911.

attraction.name: Sassoon Docks
attraction.text: One of the oldest docks in Mumbai and was the first wet dock constructed in the city. It is also one of the largest fish markets in the city. In 2017, street art transformed the fishing dock into an exhibition space.

attraction.name: Wellington Fountain
attraction.text: A small elegant marble fountain dating back to the 1860s.

attraction.name: Maharashtra Police Headquarters
attraction.text: The grand building dates back to 1876 and was built as a home for the seamen and was known as Royal Alfred Sailors Home. Built in Gothic style it was designed by Frederick William Stevens. The giant pediment at the centre of the building contains a statue of Neptune, the guardian of the seas.

attraction.name: Eros Cinema
attraction.text: A colonial-era cinema built in Art Deco style. The hall started functioning in 1938 and had a sitting capacity of 1204. It was closed down in 2016 for renovation, and was reopened in February 2024 with a 1,300-seater theatre and a 300-seater IMAX screen.

attraction.name: Nariman Point
attraction.area: at the southern end of Marine Drive
attraction.text: The area is on land reclaimed from the sea. Nariman Point is the business hub of Mumbai. However, with the change in economic conditions, many companies have shifted to other areas of Mumbai, like Parel, Worli, Bandra Kurla Complex (BKC), Andheri-Kurla Road and Powai.

attraction.name: Taraporewala Aquarium
attraction.text: It has an exotic collection of marine and fresh water life. An interesting section demonstrates various stages in the growth of a pearl and also displays exquisite pearl, and mother-of-pearl jewellery.

attraction.name: Western Railway Headquarters
attraction.text: The massive grey and white sandstone building stands opposite Churchgate station and on the northwest corner of the Oval Maidan. The building was constructed in 1899.

attraction.name: Babulnath Mandir
attraction.area: 16, Babulnath Rd, Charni Rd, Khareghat Colony, Malabar Hill
attraction.text: This temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is a well-known temple in south Mumbai. This temple is close to the beach and there is a climb of around 100 steps. It is also possible to take an elevator up to the temple.

attraction.name: Hanging Gardens
attraction.text: This terraced garden is visited on top of Malabar Hills. The park was laid out in 1881 by Ulhas Ghapokar over Bombay's main reservoir, probably to protect it from the contamination originating from the Parsi Tower of Silence. The park was renovated in 1921.

attraction.name: Lok Bhavan
attraction.text: The official residence of the Governor of Maharashtra, appointed by the President of India, formerly the Raj Bhavan. It was built upon the Bombay Castle, dating back to the 16th century, and was used in the British times as the Government House of the Bombay Presidency.

attraction.name: Walkeshwar Temple
attraction.area: Banganga Cross Ln, Teen Batti, Malabar Hill
attraction.text: This is a temple dedicated to the Hindu god, Shiva. According to legend, Lord Rama came here on his way to Lanka to reclaim his consort Sita, who was kidnapped by the Demon King, Ravana. The temple also has a tank called the Banganga. A quiet place amidst all the bustle.

restaurant.name: Bademiya Kebab Restaurant
restaurant.text: Eat on the road or in your car. Open until the early hours of the morning. The rolls are a favourite.

restaurant.name: Baghdadi
restaurant.text: Food is a mix of maintream Indian and Mughlai. Simple decor.

restaurant.name: Kailash Parbat
restaurant.text: This is a basic restaurant, serving excellent vegetarian Indian food.

restaurant.name: Gable's
restaurant.text: A restaurant that serves a good array of Goan food besides delicious Legs of Ham, Pork Chops and Steaks. Frequented by travellers, has a good British breakfast of ham, sausage, eggs and bacon.

restaurant.name: Pizza by the Bay
restaurant.text: Serves a popular soup and salad buffet lunch. Frequented by locals, both families and young adults, in the evening. Decorated in Art Deco style.

restaurant.name: Status
restaurant.text: Very good vegetarian restaurant with a nice atmosphere. No meat nor alcohol here, but you won't miss it: the food is exquisite.

restaurant.name: Aram Vada Pav
restaurant.area: Capitol Cinema Building, 126, Dr Dadabhai Naoroji Rd
restaurant.text: This hole in the wall is likely Mumbai's most famous purveyor of vada pav, the classic Mumbai snack of a deep-fried potato croquette in a fluffy bun. There's a small restaurant as well, but most people opt for takeaway.

restaurant.name: Britannia and Co
restaurant.text: This rundown restaurant, run by a partnership of geriatric brothers (by the name Kohinoor), is a South Mumbai institution, having been in existence since 1923. The signature dish is berry pulav, the recipe for which the late Mrs. Kohinoor found in Teheran while she was working with Iranian Airways.
restaurant.price: ₹400 will buy you a good lunch

restaurant.name: Pancham Puriwala
restaurant.text: Serve the best puris as the same implies with some side dishes. Not the greatest in ambience, but a very good hole-in-the-wall restaurant around here.

restaurant.name: Chetana Vegetarian Restaurant
restaurant.text: A great Gujarati and Rajasthani food restaurant. Service is ok, the atmosphere is decent. They also serve cocktails and beer. ₹450 for two.

restaurant.name: Fountain Sizzlers
restaurant.text: As the name suggests, it is famous for its sizzlers, especially among the office crowd.

restaurant.name: Trishna
restaurant.text: Famous for its seafood and patronised by locals, as well as expats.

cafe.name: Leopold Cafe
cafe.text: This place requires no introduction and is a favourite with travellers and locals alike. Serves a mix of Indian, Chinese, Persian, and Continental Food. Also serves great breakfast round the clock; it is renowned for fresh fruit juices.

cafe.name: Cafe Mondegar
cafe.text: Mondy's, as it's popularly called, serves excellent pitchers of Kingfisher, and at rock-bottom prices. Beer and wine are the only alcohols on the menu. Has a live jukebox and functions as a bar (beer and wine served) and restaurant. Food is a mix of Indian, Continental and Parsi, and the ambience is fun and low-key.

cafe.name: Cafe Basilico
cafe.text: off Colaba Causeway, near Strand cinema. This is not a budget restaurant, but it's not expensive either. Very popular with white immigrants who live in the city. Offers non-alcoholic drinks and coolers, Mediterranean-inspired food, and great dessert. Open all day.

cafe.name: Cafe Churchill
cafe.area: East West Court Building, Colaba Causeway, Apollo Bandar
cafe.text: Serves a mix of world foods (sandwiches, burgers, pasta, soups) in a very cramped location. The food is pretty good, especially the pasta. The desserts here are the best and one should not miss the Irish Baileys Chocolate Cake, which is highly recommended.

cafe.name: Cafe Royal
cafe.text: U.S. President Bill Clinton chose to eat here on his visit to India. Famous for sizzlers and other continental food.

cafe.name: Cafe Samovar
cafe.area: Inside Jehangir Art Gallery, Kala Ghoda
cafe.text: A favourite with the Mumbai art community, serving vegetarian and non-vegetarian Indian food.

cafe.name: Byculla Restaurant and Bakery
cafe.text: A typical Iranian restaurant that has been in business for just under a century.

cafe.name: Mewad ice cream
cafe.text: If you happen to be in Mumbai, it is recommended you avoid ice creams from the famous and expensive parlors and try out the cheap Mewad ice cream stalls. They are a lovely treat at their price and provide a lot of options. The vendors are found everywhere across the streets, but avoid those who appear unhygienic.

cafe.name: Cafe Mocha
cafe.text: It is a relaxed Sheesha restaurant serving heavy snacks. Very popular for dessert and coffee.

cafe.name: Trattoria
cafe.text: 24 hour coffee shop. Excellent pizzas. Can get extremely crowded on Sundays.

cafe.name: The Sassy Spoon
cafe.area: Express Towers behind Air India building
cafe.text: A mix of cuisine including Indian, Asian, and Continental dishes. Eclectic decor. Bakery associated with the restaurant next door.

cafe.name: Hard Rock Cafe
cafe.text: More club-like than most other Hard Rock Cafes worldwide. Packed with the post-office media crowd (usually between 20-30 years old), with a fair share of expats. Drinks ₹300 up. Thursdays band nights. Don't expect to get a table for a while if you go after 11PM.

photo.name: Nariman Point
photo.area: at the southern end of Marine Drive
photo.text: The area is on land reclaimed from the sea. Nariman Point is the business hub of Mumbai. However, with the change in economic conditions, many companies have shifted to other areas of Mumbai, like Parel, Worli, Bandra Kurla Complex (BKC), Andheri-Kurla Road and Powai.

photo.name: Babulnath Mandir
photo.area: 16, Babulnath Rd, Charni Rd, Khareghat Colony, Malabar Hill
photo.text: This temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is a well-known temple in south Mumbai. This temple is close to the beach and there is a climb of around 100 steps. It is also possible to take an elevator up to the temple.

photo.name: Hanging Gardens
photo.text: This terraced garden is visited on top of Malabar Hills. The park was laid out in 1881 by Ulhas Ghapokar over Bombay's main reservoir, probably to protect it from the contamination originating from the Parsi Tower of Silence. The park was renovated in 1921.

photo.name: Dhobi Ghat
photo.text: The famous open-air laundry place in Mumbai. Built in 1890, the washers in Dhobi Ghat work in the open to clean clothes and linens from Mumbai's hotels and hospitals. There are rows of open-air concrete wash pens, each fitted with its own flogging stone.

photo.name: Joseph Baptista Gardens
photo.text: A park atop Bhandarwada Hill and offers a panoramic view of the Mumbai Harbour and the southern business district of the city. Beneath the gardens is a water reservoir, constructed between 1880–1884. The park is frequented by neighbourhood residents.

photo.name: Sewri Flamingo Point
photo.text: It has large areas of mudflats which are not only a safe habitat for flamingoes in winter but also have adequate food availability. A large number of flamingos reach along with their babies from their breeding area, Rann of Kutch, to Sewri every year. They arrive and stay between the month of October to March.

photo.name: Horniman Circle Gardens
photo.text: A circular open space covering an area of 12,081 square yards at the heart of Mumbai's Fort area. Construction of the garden started in 1921 and was completed after 12 years. After 1942 the garden lost its glory and was used as a dumping area of coconut shells.

photo.name: Coastal Road Promenade
photo.text: The newest promenade of Mumbai that runs along the city's Coastal Road from Worli to Malabar Hill. Unfortunately, there are no trees along the promenade, making the experience more Dubai-like.

Bengaluru.name: Bengaluru
Bengaluru.tagline: Bengaluru, formerly Bangalore, is the largest city in southern India and the capital of the state of Karnataka.

info.intro: Bengaluru, formerly Bangalore, is the largest city in southern India and the capital of the state of Karnataka. A cosmopolitan city, Bengaluru was developed around what was once a mud fort of a feudal lord. The city has a population of nearly 13 million (2025), making it India's fourth-largest city. Known worldwide as the "Silicon Valley of India", Bengaluru is at the core of India's information technology (IT) industry. In addition, the city is nicknamed the "Garden City" for its large array of parks and greenery.
info.understand: Bengaluru (BAYNG-guh-LOO-roo) is a bustling metropolis with a large working population from different parts of India. The city's fast-paced culture provides a sharp contrast to much of the rest of India. The earliest records of a place named "Bengaluru" are found in a ninth-century temple in present-day South Bengaluru. A popular myth explaining the name is that it originated from Benda Kaal Uru (Town of Boiled Beans). The story is told that the name was given to the city by King Vira Ballala, who, while lost in the area, was offered boiled beans by an old woman. The name was officially changed from Bangalore to Bengaluru in 2014. Although both names are common ever since, people who use "Bangalore" are generally non-Kannada speakers, whereas "Bengaluru" users primarily speak Kannada.
info.get_in: Bookings can be done at either the railway stations or at the Indian Railways booking counters in major commercial and residential areas. Booking can also be done online. As with all Indian railway travel, have some patience for delays. Trains are usually on time (within 20 min of scheduled time), but can sometimes be late. A digital departure board in the station will tell you what platform your train is on and what time it leaves. Travelling from Mumbai to Bengaluru by train takes a long time (24 hr or so). Buses are comparatively faster and take 18-20 hr, provided there are no traffic jams in Mumbai and Pune en route. Effective travel time by train or bus is long. Air travel is recommended for traveling between Mumbai and Bengaluru, the duration of which is about 90 min. Low-cost airlines charge the same fare as AC train or Volvo bus.
info.get_around: Traffic in Bengaluru is generally appalling: it's often ranked as one of India's most congested cities. Allow plenty of time to get around, especially anywhere near rush hour. Heavy rains often cause flooding that can bring traffic to a complete standstill. The schedules of the metro and buses are integrated into Google Maps. The Namma Metro is an efficient cross-city rail service in Bengaluru that provides the only realistic way to escape the traffic, but its coverage of the city remains limited. As of August 2025, there are three lines: Green Line Purple Line (Whitefield (Kadugodi)–Challaghatta) Yellow Line (Rashtreeya Vidyalaya (RV) Road-Bommasandra) Tickets can be bought at any station, either from manned counters (cash accepted) or ticketing machines (UPI only). Fares depend on the number of stations you travel. Minimum fare is ₹10 and maximum is ₹90.
info.stay_safe: Bengaluru is a relatively safe city at that time. However, most of Bengaluru practically shuts down a little before midnight, even very safe residential areas can be very desolate by 11PM. In the morning, people start getting out from 5AM or 6AM, but it's usually still dark outside at that time, so exercise caution if you are in an unfamiliar area. Some of the lower-income areas can be somewhat unsafe once it gets dark. Exercising caution and good sense will increase your chances of staying safe. It is not advisable to walk alone along deserted alleyways or lanes after dark. Avoid doing so in areas that you are not sure are reasonably safe. Avoid using an auto-rickshaw if the driver is not alone, especially at night. Do not flaunt jewellery, high-end mobile phones, laptops, watches etc. Do not withdraw large amounts of cash from ATMs in deserted areas.

attraction.name: Cubbon Park
attraction.text: A nice forested area in the city centre. The entrance from Queen's Statue forms the tourist attraction owing to the presence of the Government Aquarium and Bal Bhavan, a play area for kids. Puttaani Express a small toy train for kids, runs inside the Bal Bhavan, attracting kids from far and near.

attraction.name: Attara Kacheri
attraction.text: A two-storey neoclassical red-painted stone and brick building, hosting the High Court of Karnataka. It was a secretariat of eighteen departments, built under the reign of king Devaraja Wadiyar II in 1701. The main structure of the building is surrounded on all sides by porticoes and verandahs.

attraction.name: General Post Office
attraction.text: Its first floor contains a philatelic museum.

attraction.name: Lok Bhavan
attraction.text: The official residence of the Governor of Karnataka, appointed by the President of India, formerly the Raj Bhavan. Built by Sir Mark Cubbon between 1840 and 1842, it was originally home to the Resident or Commissioner that was in subsidiary alliance with the Kingdom of Mysore.
attraction.image: Independence day at Raj Bhavan, Bangalore (2025) 86.jpg

attraction.name: Vidhana Soudha
attraction.text: This granite building houses the Legislative Assembly of Karnataka. It was built during the tenure of K. Hanumanthaiya, Chief Minister of Mysore State. A marvel of neo-Dravidian architecture, and one of the most imposing buildings in India.

attraction.name: Vikasa Soudha
attraction.text: Located next to Vidhana Soudha, built in the same classic style. It was inaugurated in 2005. General public and tourists are not allowed to enter the premises. It can only be viewed from outside the boundary walls.

attraction.name: Visvesvaraya Centre
attraction.text: A government office complex, built on the site of the house of Sir M. Visvesvaraya after his death. Initially constructed for the Life Insurance Corporation (LIC), it was later bought by the state government to house government offices.

attraction.name: Visvesvaraya Industrial & Technological Museum
attraction.text: Contains many fun learning activities and exhibitions that can be enjoyed by adults and children. Most exhibits are based on simple science, but some have industrial applications. For general visitors entry fee is ₹40.

attraction.name: Gallery G
attraction.text: Provides informed access to art and consultancy services for investors, architects and interior designers, and organises travelling art shows.

attraction.name: Government Aquarium
attraction.area: at the entrance of Cubbon Park, close to VITM
attraction.text: The second largest aquarium in India. It has a variety of exotic cultivable as well as marine fishes on display, including include eels, angelfish, glowlight tetra, hockey stick tetra, red-tail shark, catla, Indian tiger barb, mahseer, freshwater prawns, blue gourami, pearl gourami, goldfish, moon tail etc.
attraction.price: ₹150 per head for adults, ₹5 per head for students upto 10th standard, free for...

attraction.name: Government Museum
attraction.text: Established in 1865, the museum is flanked by the Visvesvaraya Industrial & Technological Museum and the Venkatappa Art Gallery. It is an archaeological museum with a rare collection of archaeological and geological artefacts, including old jewellery, sculpture, coins and inscriptions.

attraction.name: Kingfisher Towers
attraction.text: Probably the most famous high-rise residential building in Bengaluru, despite not being the tallest in the city. The top of the building is occupied by a mansion, which is one of the few instances of a "building atop a building" in India.

restaurant.name: Adyar Ananda Bhavan
restaurant.text: This is mostly a vegetarian breakfast and sweet shop. It has many native foods such as dosa, idli, vada and chutney. It has a wide range of Indian sweets such as jalebis and rasgullas.

restaurant.name: Mavalli Tiffin Room
restaurant.text: One of the very old traditional breakfast places in Bengaluru. There are a few people who have been having their breakfast at MTR every day for the past 15 years. Traditional 12-course Karnataka lunches are also available here for around ₹90 per head. Rava idlis, dosas and bisi bele bath are excellent.
restaurant.hours: Closed between 2:45-3:30PM. Expect a long wait on weekends, advance...
restaurant.image: Mavalli Tiffin Room (6), Lalbagh Road, Bengaluru.jpg

restaurant.name: Vidyarthi Bhavan
restaurant.text: Literally a "Student House", Vidyarthi Bhavan is a very old and traditional vegetarian breakfast place, and a gastronomic haven, offering some of the best masala dosas in the world. This quaint little place is so famous that it has not even bothered to change its age-old sign board, and who needs it anyway.

restaurant.name: Bobby-da-Dhaba
restaurant.area: Near Lavanya Theatre, St John's Road, Near Ulsoor
restaurant.text: The food is good (albeit slightly oily). It basically serves paranthas (with lots of butter), chaach, kheer and a number of side dishes (most notable being their shahi paneer and rajma). You may have to wait for a while in case it is full.

restaurant.name: Coconut Grove
restaurant.text: Appams and Kerala parottas with a chicken sauce dish. Their lunch offer for ₹80 is also really good. A pretty good choice for reasonably priced quality seafood. Coco-Grove the outdoor 'beer cafe' extension is also worth a look.

restaurant.name: Koshy's
restaurant.text: A Bengaluru institution, serving a smattering of Western favorites (like fish and chips) along with the usual South Indian fare in a bohemian-for-India atmosphere. On weekends, they serve up greasy Western-style breakfast, including omelettes and Bombay (i.e, French) Toast.

restaurant.name: Rahhams Families
restaurant.text: Serves the kind of biryani that is the Bengaluru original. It is midway on MM Rd, and hard to miss because of the crowds that throng its takeaway counter. One visits Richies only for the food—tables and chairs made of synthetic wood, and dim light from gaudy chandeliers don’t exactly make for great ambiance.

restaurant.name: Central Tiffin Room (CTR)
restaurant.text: Another landmark hotel, dishing out some divine 'Benne masala dosa', which literally melts in the mouth. Famous for its butter masala dosa.

restaurant.name: Halli Mane
restaurant.text: Truly authentic and traditional Kannada style food.

restaurant.name: Hotel Janatha
restaurant.text: Another great place, famous for its butter masala dosas and vadas.

restaurant.name: Veena Stores
restaurant.text: This place has some of the best Idlis and Vadas in this part of the world. They also make other dishes but Idli and Vada are mainstay. Don't expect to sit and eat because there is no seating. Stand and eat. Best time to go is mornings for breakfast before they run out of the day's stock.

restaurant.name: Manjit ka Dhaba
restaurant.area: 107, 1st Floor, Wheeler Road, Near Railway Cross, Cox Town
restaurant.text: Budget dhaba. Tasty parathas (with butter) and couple of assorted vegetable curry options. Lassi. Don't expect ambience in dhabas.

cafe.name: Oh! Calcutta
cafe.text: Part of a chain of restaurants across the country, and the best Bengali food available in the city albeit pricier than the other options.

cafe.name: Brahmin's Coffee Bar
cafe.text: Famous for idli, vada and its delicious chutney. You also get khaarabath. Don't expect sambar for the vada here.

cafe.name: The Rameshwaram Cafe @ Indiranagar
cafe.text: A veritable shrine to south Indian food, all polished black marble. Particularly famous for their ultra crispy ghee dosas but it's all good, try the Kanchipuram idlis for something a little different. Standing tables only and gets packed late at night.

cafe.name: Café Coffee Day
cafe.text: Popularly known as CCD. Established in 1996, at Brigade Road, the chain has over 1,000 cafes throughout India. It is found all over Bengaluru.

cafe.name: The Adiga's chain
cafe.text: Restaurants to the south of Bengaluru. Prominent among them are in: Jayanagar 4th Block, take the road facing BHS First Grade College, Basavanagudi.

cafe.name: Beijing Bites
cafe.text: Chain restaurant inspired by Chinese & Thai cuisines, spread across Bengaluru.

cafe.name: Corner House
cafe.area: Residency Rd, BTM Rd, Koramangala, Airport Rd, Whitefield Rd,...
cafe.text: One of the best ice cream parlours offering a variety of treats. Their famed 'Death by Chocolate' (popularly known as DBC) is a must for all chocolate lovers and has attained a cult status.

cafe.name: Nandini
cafe.text: The Andhra fast food chain serves some excellent biriyani and chicken dishes.

cafe.name: New Shanti Sagar
cafe.text: This is a reasonably reliable chain of vegetarian south Indian restaurants. Branches scattered all over the city, notably in Koramangala Jayanagar, Domlur. ₹50-200.

cafe.name: The Rameshwaram Cafe
cafe.text: A well-known restaurant chain famous for its extra crispy ghee dosas. Standing room only and hugely popular, all food is made to order so at peak meal times you may need to wait for an hour or longer.

cafe.name: Savera Tea Shop
cafe.text: 24 hr tea shops near Russell Market in Shivajinagar and on MG Rd. Good place to go for a cup of tea in the dead of the night. Serves tea, Suleimani (honey+lemon) tea and a variety of biscuits. ₹3-15

cafe.name: SLV chain
cafe.text: Prominent among them are in: Banashankari 2nd stage, opposite BDA park and the one in J.P.Nagar 2nd Phase near Ragigudda Temple

photo.name: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
photo.text: Built during the reigns of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, the botanical garden is home to numerous wild species of birds and other wildlife. The garden also has a lake adjoining a large rock is home to some water birds.

photo.name: Muthyala Maduvu
photo.text: Known for its waterfall and the mountain ranges it overlooks. It has a rich concentration of birds owing to the presence of the waterfall. Trekking enthusiasts also visited the mountain ranges, and trekking is a major adventure sport.

photo.name: Thottikallu Falls
photo.text: A waterfall visited by locals during weekends. Unfortunately, there's actually no entry to the waterfall, and trespassers are fined or prosecuted.

photo.name: Ulsoor Lake
photo.text: One of the biggest lakes in Bengaluru, with several islands. There's a watch tower with a Chinese bell on the lake.

photo.name: Hebbal Lake
photo.area: at the interchange of NH 44 and NH 75
photo.text: One of the three lakes created in 1537 during the rule of Kempe Gowda.

photo.name: Hesaraghatta Lake
photo.text: A freshwater lake created in 1894 across the Arkavati River to meet the drinking water needs of the city. It is an integral part of the Greater Hesaraghatta Grassland Conservation Reserve.

photo.name: Agara Lake
photo.text: One of the most well-maintained lakes of Bengaluru. It is surrounded by a walking and cycling track, with a park at the north end.

photo.name: Madiwala Lake
photo.text: One of the biggest lakes in Bengaluru and a grave example of water pollution. The water was fit for drinking till the early 1990s, when the industrial waste and sewage made it unsafe. Despite this, the lake sees a huge number of spot-billed pelicans migrating in the winter, especially in November and December.

photo.name: Bellandur Lake
photo.text: Although it has been severely impacted by the bane of urbanisation, the lake is still home to a diverse species of birds, like herons, egrets, wagtails, kites, sandpipers, etc.

photo.name: Varthur Lake
photo.text: An integral part of the city, although unplanned urbanisation and industrialisation have led to its contamination, similar to the Bellandur Lake. It has suffered from eutrophication and is now home to diverse algae.

photo.name: Lumbini Garden
photo.text: A public park along the Nagawara Lake. It contains an eco-friendly boating park and a artificial beach and children's pool.

Kolkata.name: Kolkata
Kolkata.tagline: Kolkata, formerly and still fondly called Calcutta, is the largest city in eastern India and the capital of the state...

info.intro: Kolkata, formerly and still fondly called Calcutta, is the largest city in eastern India and the capital of the state of West Bengal. Once the capital of India till 1911, Kolkata lies on the Hooghly River in South Bengal. Greater Kolkata has a population of over 22.5 million (2025), making it one of the world's largest cities. Kolkata is an "in your face" city that shocks and charms the unsuspecting visitor. Long known as the cultural capital of India and home to the Bengali Renaissance, the "City of Joy" (the sobriquet became more famous after the publication of a novel of the same name) continues to spawn generations of poets, writers, film directors and Nobel Prize winners.
info.understand: Kolkata is the main financial and commercial hub of eastern India. Once the administrative centre of the British Raj in South Asia, Kolkata is often considered the "cultural capital" of India due to its importance in modern Indian history. Name The city has been known by various names. The original Bengali name is Kolikātā, which is said to be derived from Kālīkhyetro, the "land of goddess Kali". Another theory is that the place used to specialise in quicklime and coir rope. Whatever its origins, the British anglicised it to "Calcutta" and the Bengali name evolved into Kolkātā or Kōlkātā. In 2001, the then-left Government of West Bengal changed the official name from "Calcutta" to "Kolkata", reflecting the contemporary name. While the anglicised name is considered archaic these days, people still use it fondly to invoke the days of yore.
info.get_in: Although the airport is large and spacious, after immigration it lacks the facilities generally associated with busy international airports; there is no cafe, only one sit-down restaurant, very limited number of small shops, and no free Wi-Fi. Toilets are also sparse and far apart. The airport has a well-established facility of prepaid taxis and air-conditioned buses connecting it to the city centre. Parking facilities at the airport terminal include two underground parking levels accommodating 3,000 cars, and outdoor car parking which can handle an additional 2,000 cars. DigiYatra facility is available at departure gates 2B and 3A, security hold area 1, 2 and 3 and boarding gates 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 and 23. Transport options to central Kolkata: By bus: State-run air-conditioned buses are available to get into the city centre.
info.get_around: Road transport shuts down in some places for roadworks and during Durga Puja. However, metro is usually available in those occasions. Kolkata has a very comprehensive public transport network. Despite residents' perpetual grumbling about unreliability, public transport is often the best option for getting anywhere for visitors and residents alike. In general, use metro or suburban rail as they are separated from the city's road traffic, and use auto-rickshaws and taxis for last-mile connectivity. Buses are fine on some roads where metro does not ply, like APC Road, Gariahat Road and Rashbehari Avenue. Often called the lifeline of Kolkata, the Kolkata Metro is the fastest, cleanest and most efficient mode of transport the city has to offer.
info.stay_safe: For any emergency dial. This number connects to police, fire, ambulance, women and child helplines as well as the coast guard for incidents on the river. You will be asked which of these services you require before being connected to the relevant operator. Kolkata is one of the safest cities in India. People here are friendly and helpful and accept people of different cultures warmly. Taking normal precautions for the safe keeping of your personal possessions is enough, as you would do in any Indian city. Police The Kolkata Police (KP) is responsible for policing the city except New Town and Salt Lake, which are the responsibility of the Bidhannagar City Police, and much of the Northern Suburbs, which are the responsibility of the Barrackpore Police Commissionerate. In addition to these, the Kolkata Metro and suburban railways are patrolled by the Railway Protection Force (RPF).

attraction.name: Dhapa
attraction.text: Despite being a major landfill site where the solid waste are dumped, more than 40% of the green vegetables in the city's markets come from here, being a prominent example of peri-urban agriculture in Kolkata.

attraction.name: Forum Atmosphere
attraction.text: A luxury residential building, consisting of two tower blocks and a structure called "Deya" connecting the two. Deya is the world's first residential floating sky sculpture, and it houses the residents' community and recreational facilities, including a swimming pool, gymnasium, spas, running track, sporting...

attraction.name: Kolkata Leather Complex
attraction.text: An industrial complex and the centre of leather-tanning business of the metropolis, fondly known as chormonogorī. It has approximately 500 tanneries, which account for 22-25% of all the tanning in India.

attraction.name: New Town Gate
attraction.area: Major Arterial Rd, Narkelbagan, Action Area I
attraction.text: An arch monument in New Town and one of the most iconic structures in Kolkata. The structure consists of a single ring supported by two parabolic arches from four sides of the Narkelbagan intersection. The ring houses a restaurant, an observation deck, as well as souvenir shops.
attraction.price: Free for children below 3, ₹100 per adult

attraction.name: Pedestrian Plaza
attraction.text: A pedestrian zone, stretched from Infinity Benchmark to RDB Boulevard. Opened in September 2023 with a vibe of New York's famous intersection, this cyberpunky area has become a hangout spot for social media reels. There are tall obelisks on both sides, and walking spaces in between.

attraction.name: Bengal Village
attraction.text: An exhibition containing models depicting the daily life of rural Bengal.

attraction.name: Butterfly Garden
attraction.text: It consists of a large dome to enclose a plant habitat consisting of different species of flowering annuals and perennials that support a large range of butterflies organised around a circular body of water.
attraction.image: Dome shaped arena for culturing butterfly WLB 0082.jpg

attraction.name: Ghum railway station
attraction.text: A dummy railway station with a toy train of the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway. You can get into the train to get a feeling of the Darjeeling Hills. It costs ₹10 per head for photoshoot inside the train.

attraction.name: Mask Garden
attraction.text: An open-air collection of masks from various parts of the world, especially from various states of India, especially from West Bengal.

attraction.name: Promenade
attraction.text: The spine of Eco Park is a paved pathway lined with coconut trees. It is designed to enjoy the waterbody. There's a massive Solar Dome and a replica of the Eiffel Tower along the promenade.

attraction.name: Rose Garden
attraction.text: A long walking path with varieties of roses at both sides.

attraction.name: Solar Dome
attraction.text: A dome-shaped structure that houses a museum about solar energy and its use in daily life. It has a guided tour with humanoid robots. The dome also houses a planetarium, marine aquarium, and an observation deck.
attraction.price: ₹200 for adults, ₹100 for group tours with over 30 students, free for children...

restaurant.name: Anadi Cabin
restaurant.text: Known for Mughlai paratha.
restaurant.image: Anadi Cabin - Restaurant - 9A Chowringhee Road - Kolkata 2015-01-30 5705.JPG

restaurant.name: Dacres Lane
restaurant.text: A popular alley for lunch by commuters.

restaurant.name: Nizam's
restaurant.text: Opened in 1932, the restaurant is an unpretentious place that is famous for 'Muslim' food and lays claim to be the place where Kathi Rolls were invented, it is still considered to make the best ones. The roll initially became popular among the BBD Bagh officers during lunch time, then became an iconic food of Kolkata.

restaurant.name: Bhim Chandra Nag
restaurant.text: The 200-year-old shop is famous for sandesh. It is the inventor of le ikeni, named after the wife of Lord Canning, the then-Viceroy of India.
restaurant.image: Bhim Chandra Nag sweet shop at Bowbazar, Kolkata, WB.jpg

restaurant.name: Arsalan Restaurant & Caterer
restaurant.text: Biryani and Mughlai food. Popular items: firni, mutton kosha, mutton boti kebab, chicken chatpata, mutton biryani, egg chicken roll.

restaurant.name: Charnock's
restaurant.text: Continental, Bengali, North Indian cuisine. Drinks served.

restaurant.name: OG by the Lake
restaurant.text: Outdoor seating, and a glasshouse with floral-deck ambiance. Offers Asian, Continental, Italian and North Indian food. Handmade mocktails and coffee served.

restaurant.name: Shiraz Golden Restaurant
restaurant.text: Biryani and Mughlai food. The Anandapur branch of the popular restaurant at Park Street.

restaurant.name: Beijing Restaurant
restaurant.text: Chinese cuisine. Drinks served.

restaurant.name: Big Boss
restaurant.text: Chinese cuisine. Drinks served.

restaurant.name: Chung-Wah
restaurant.text: One of the oldest and best places to sample Chinese food. Drinks served.

restaurant.name: Drive Inn
restaurant.text: An outdoor restaurant offering a wide range of good vegetarian and non-vegetarian fare (Indian/Chinese). AC area available, staff speaks good English and is friendly.

cafe.name: Flurys
cafe.text: A popular and stylish café serving a good variety of baked goods and various coffees, sandwiches and entrees. A great place for breakfast or lunch. Baked goods ₹80-₹100, drinks ₹80, meals ₹600-₹1000.
cafe.image: Flurys, Park Street, Kolkata, Interior, Sales Counter.jpg

cafe.name: Indian Coffee House
cafe.text: A venerable old establishment run by the Indian Coffee Workers Co-op Society. The high ceilings, peeling paintwork, skylights and workers in traditional uniforms create an image straight out of the 1920s or 1930s movie. In addition, the coffee (and the food) is good and cheap.

cafe.name: Cafe Amari
cafe.text: A café with the French colonial vibe of Pondicherry, It has a strong coffee selection of pour-over V60 and frappés, fresh juices and bakery treats like butter croissants, Korean-style buns and Boston crème doughnuts.

cafe.name: Calcutta Art Café
cafe.text: Known for its lavish interior with chequered floors, bricked walls and stained-glass hurricane lamps. It blends modernity with vintage.

cafe.name: Blue Sky Cafe
cafe.text: The food is cheap, the place is clean and service is truly fantastic. Great if you are on an extended stay as they offer both Indian and some Western food. You will not find nicer waiters anywhere. Try the fresh squeezed juices.

cafe.name: Mission Cafe
cafe.text: Vegetarian fast food spot. Dosa, chaats and curry served at high tables. The cafe is known for its chola-bhatura, a chickpea dish served in a phuchka shell. Turnover fast here, not even stools to sit on, but it is nonetheless tasty.

cafe.name: Raj's Spanish Cafe
cafe.text: Serves breakfast and espresso based coffees. Mexican, pizza, and other Western staples.

cafe.name: Baithak Khana Cafe
cafe.text: A family-owned heritage café, with its walls depicting Kolkata's history. It was once a meeting spot for the members of the Young Bengal Movement led by Derozio, and was originally owned by Rev. Krishna Mohan Banerjee, himself a member of the movement.

cafe.name: Mitra Cafe
cafe.text: North Indian fast food outlet famous for its brain chop. Fish Kaviraji, brain chop, Chicken Kaviraji, Mutton Kaviraji, mutton cutlets, fries, Prawn Kaviraji. Also go for the various chops, cutlets or Afghani.

cafe.name: Only 4 Chinese Gazab
cafe.text: Quality Indian Chinese and great pork items. Also, try their Darsaan with vanilla ice cream.

cafe.name: Cha Bar
cafe.area: 2nd floor, Oxford Book Store, Park Street
cafe.text: A modern and chic cafe with a great selection of teas, including herbal, smoothies. Cha Bar also sells coffee, but this is of mediocre quality. A large window offers views of street life below, while the books provide a literary dimension. Cha Bar is an excellent place for a budding writer or a day dreamer.

cafe.name: Olive Café & Bar
cafe.text: Mediterranean charm and handmade cocktails.

photo.name: Butterfly Garden
photo.text: It consists of a large dome to enclose a plant habitat consisting of different species of flowering annuals and perennials that support a large range of butterflies organised around a circular body of water.
photo.image: Dome shaped arena for culturing butterfly WLB 0082.jpg

photo.name: Mask Garden
photo.text: An open-air collection of masks from various parts of the world, especially from various states of India, especially from West Bengal.

photo.name: Promenade
photo.text: The spine of Eco Park is a paved pathway lined with coconut trees. It is designed to enjoy the waterbody. There's a massive Solar Dome and a replica of the Eiffel Tower along the promenade.

photo.name: Rose Garden
photo.text: A long walking path with varieties of roses at both sides.

photo.name: Tropical Tree Garden
photo.text: Contains a piece of the tropical forest of Bengal.

photo.name: Babughat
photo.text: The second-oldest surviving ghat in Kolkata, originally named "Baboo Raj Chandra Ghat" after the husband of Rashmoni Dasi, better known as Rani Rashmoni. She built it in 1830 in memory of her late husband. The landing berth of the ghat has a tall colonial structure, with a fine Doric style pavilion and tall columns.

photo.name: Tazaung
photo.text: A Buddhist pagoda, set in a small lake. Lord Dalhousie brought the pagoda from Prome in Burma (present-day Pyay in Myanmar) and erected here in 1854.

photo.name: Outram Ghat
photo.text: One of Kolkata's premier riverside entertainment spots. The place is a long stretch with a grand view of the river and Vidyasagar Setu nearby. There are numerous eateries. One can also have a ride in a country boat. The ghat is used for bathing and religious ceremonies.

photo.name: Prinsep Ghat
photo.text: Often misspelt "Princep Ghat", the memorial ghat is named after James Prinsep, a 19th century East India Company official best known as a historical scholar. It gives an excellent view of the Hooghly River and Vidyasagar Setu.

photo.name: Nimtala Ghat
photo.text: One of the largest crematoria in India, and one of the holiest for Hindus, similar to the Manikarnika Ghat in Varanasi. It is believed that the soul attains moksha in this crematorium, which breaks the cycle of birth and death. So, people across the country come here for the cremation of their loved ones.

photo.name: Mayer Ghat
photo.text: An old bathing ghat where Sarada Devi, the wife of Sri Ramakrishna, used to bathe.
photo.image: Mayer Ghat at dusk during Corona crisis 01.jpg

photo.name: Mohun Bagan Memorial
photo.text: A memorial housed in the palace that gave birth to one of Kolkata's premier football clubs. The name "Mohun Bagan" comes from that garden that belonged to Gopi Mohun Deb of the Sovabazar Raj family, which was replaced by the present building built by jute merchant Kirti Chandra Mitra.

Chennai.name: Chennai
Chennai.tagline: Chennai, formerly Madras, is the largest coastal city in southern India and the capital of the state of Tamil Nadu.

info.intro: Chennai, formerly Madras, is the largest coastal city in southern India and the capital of the state of Tamil Nadu. It is on the east coast of peninsular India. Though Chennai traces its history to Fort St George and the adjoining village of Madrasapattinam founded by the British East India Company in 1640, some residential districts of the city are older. With a metropolitan population of over 11 million (2025), Chennai is the fifth-largest city in India, and the second-largest in southern India after Bengaluru.
info.understand: Name The name "Madras" was adopted during the British rule. The Tamil Nadu government changed it to Chennai in 1996, claiming that Chennai is the original name of the city. However, the origin of both names are uncertain. As per local legend, the name "Madras" comes from "Madrasapattinam" and the name "Chennai" from "Chennapattinam". Madrasapattinam was the name of the British settlement, and Chennapattinam was a fishing village nearby. However, it is not clear if the village was there beforehand or grew up around Madrasapattinam. As the settlements grew, the locations of "Chennapattinam" and "Madrasapattinam" became confused as the two settlements merged into a single town. It is also believed that early Portuguese voyagers may have called the area Madre de Sois after an early settler, or Madre de Deus after an early church (of St. Mary), which corrupted to "Madras".
info.get_in: By metro The Blue Line of the Chennai Metro connects the airport to MGR Chennai Central. There's also an inter-corridor service along the Green Line that follows the Blue Line from Airport to Alandur. By taxi Use the prepaid taxi to reach the central business district. Every terminal has many taxi booths when you leave the airport. Fast Track has the best rep, figure on around ₹560 to the city centre for a Toyota Innova or equivalent. The fares differ for the international and domestic terminals though the terminals are next to each other. You can either choose the standard taxis (black with yellow tops) or the private call-taxi (which can come in any colour). It is better to have some loose change when paying at the counters. The taxi number is written on your charge slip. One copy is for the passenger while the other is for the driver to collect the fare from the counter.
info.get_around: Getting around the heart of Chennai city often takes time, due to traffic and heavy congestion. So it is advisable to plan your journey accordingly. Travelling within Chennai is not so cheap by Indian metropolitan standards, and is quite cheap by European and USA standards. Chennai One is a combined route planner and ticketing app. It integrates city buses, the metro, suburban trains, and taxis. Chennai has a suburban railway network. There are six suburban lines as of June 2023: North Line South Line South West Line West Line West North Line West South Line The suburban trains are generally reliable and fast. The frequency of suburban trains is generally good and it is advisable to take a first-class ticket during peak hours. Trains offer a reliable alternative to quickly reach your destination when compared to buses which might get trapped in traffic jams.
info.stay_safe: Chennai is generally a safer area of India in terms of crime, although pickpocketing, muggings, and robberies sporadically occur. Keep your doors and windows shut and locked at night and do not carry or display large amounts of cash if possible. It is advisable for women, especially unaccompanied ones, to dress modestly and limit their interaction with unfamiliar local men. Foreigners are generally overcharged by autorickshaws simply because they are ignorant of the prevailing fares. It is necessary to confirm whether the driver knows the exact destination and to fix the fare before boarding. 'Autos', as autorickshaws are known in Chennai, are notorious for fleecing customers, tourists and locals alike. Be alert to your surroundings and watch where you step, especially if you get caught in a large crowd where it is difficult to look at what is in front of you.

attraction.name: Madhavaram Botanical Garden
attraction.text: The largest botanical garden, set up by the Department of Horticulture in 2018. The garden is broadly divided into sections for fruits, medicinal plants, indoor plants, cacti and ornamental arboretum, besides one for protected cultivation.

attraction.name: Victoria Public Hall
attraction.text: One of the finest examples of British architecture in Chennai and was built to commemorate the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria. Constructed with red brick and painted with lime mortar, the rectangular building has an Italianate tower capped by a Travancore-style roof.

attraction.name: Fort St. George
attraction.text: It was established as the East India Company's fortified foothold in Madras and it was from this small trading post (or 'factory' as it was then known) that British influence spread throughout India. The establishment of Fort St. George marked the birth of the new city that is Madras, in the year 1640.
attraction.price: Fort Museum: children under 15 years free, Indians ₹5, foreigners US$20

attraction.name: Madras High Court
attraction.text: The third-oldest high court in India and an example of Indo-Saracenic architecture. Covering, the court complex is one of the largest in the world.

attraction.name: Victory War Memorial
attraction.text: The memorial is erected in memory of those from the erstwhile Madras Presidency who died in world wars. The memorial also has inscriptions on 1948 Kashmir Aggression, 1962 War with China and the Indo-Pakistan War.

attraction.name: Armenian Church
attraction.text: Constructed in 1712 and reconstructed in 1772. The graves of about 350 Armenians have been laid out throughout the Church. The founder, publisher and editor of the world's first Armenian periodical "Azdarar", Reverend Haroutiun Shmavonian, is buried here.

attraction.name: St. Mary's Church
attraction.text: This is one of the oldest surviving churches built by the British in India. This is the first British church in India and the oldest Anglican church in the East. Designed by William Dixon, the then Master Gunner of the Fort, it was constructed under the supervision of Governor Streynsham Master.

attraction.name: Kalikambal Temple
attraction.text: Dedicated to Kalikambal and Kamateswarar, this temple was built close to sea shore but was relocated in 1640 AD. The great Maratha ruler Shivaji came in the temple to worship on 3 October 1667.

attraction.name: Royapuram Fire Temple
attraction.text: A Parsi fire temple built in 1910.

attraction.name: Ripon Building
attraction.text: The rectangular building built in Neoclassical style houses the office of the Corporation of Chennai, the civic body that governs the city of Chennai. The building was designed by G. T. S. Harris and was constructed between 1909 and 1913.

attraction.name: Government Museum
attraction.text: Pantheon Rd, Egmore. Established in 1857, the Government Museum of Chennai is one of the popular tourist destinations in the city. It is a multi-purpose State Government Museum in Egmore, which is in the heart of the city, spreading over an area of 16.25 acres (7 ha) of land.
attraction.hours: 9:30AM-5PM except holidays. A free guide service is available at 11AM and 3PM.

attraction.name: Integral Coach Factory
attraction.text: A railway coach manufacturing unit of the Indian Railways, which has a Rail Museum. The Regional Rail Museum is situated near ICF, Perambur, Chennai amidst the New Avadi Road/Anna Nagar Round Tana/ICF Bus Terminus and Villivakkam.

restaurant.name: Benjarong
restaurant.text: The authentic flavour of Thailand. Seating capacity 68.

restaurant.name: Little Italy
restaurant.text: Italian restaurant. Italian classic cuisine with a perfect wine. Chef's favourites: Pizza Mellino, Pasta del Fattore and In Wines- Brunello di Montalcino.

restaurant.name: Prego
restaurant.text: Gourmet Italian dining, replaced Patio.

restaurant.name: Teppan
restaurant.text: Hibachi style, the cook prepares your meal with a show right in front of you. Very entertaining especially for younger diners. Excellent sushi and sashimi. ₹2000 for a meal for two.

restaurant.name: Don Pepes
restaurant.text: Mexican. Above Hot Breads as an extension, they are best known for their fajitas (sizzlers) and enchiladas (a tortilla wrap with some Mexican rice).

restaurant.name: Cream Centre
restaurant.area: 55, 2nd Main Road, Raja Annamalaipuram (near Kaliappa Hospital)
restaurant.text: Cream Centre offers a wide range of vegetarian food choices- North Indian and Mexican, to American, Italian and even Lebanese. Nachos, Channa Bhatura, American Corn Cheese Ball, Sizzlers & Sizzling Brownie. A specialty here is the Mera Thali, where you have a choice of dishes from which you can make your own thali.

restaurant.name: Entree Restaurant
restaurant.area: Emall hotel, Express Avenue Mall, Gate No 1, Pattullous Rd, Anna Salai
restaurant.text: 100% vegetarian multi-cuisine restaurant. Serves fare from all around the world - Thai soup, Mexican main course, Indian spices tadka, French pastry for desserts.

restaurant.name: Copper Chimney
restaurant.area: 74, Cathedral Road, Gopalapuram (opposite the Chola Sheraton)
restaurant.text: Mainly North Indian and Iranian inspired dish. Specialities: Bagani Bahar, Paneer Musselum.

restaurant.name: Bella Ciao
restaurant.area: Lounge Beach Garden, #4, Shri Krishna Enclave, Kottivakkam
restaurant.text: Italian-owned and run, authentic Italian food. The famous wood fired oven pizza, home made pastas, steaks and salads.

restaurant.name: The Great Kabab Factory
restaurant.area: Radisson G R T Hotel, G.S.T. Road, St Thomas Mount
restaurant.text: Specialities: Galoutti Kabab, Tangri and Murgh Malai Kababs, Fish and Mutton Kababs. They serve alcohol and have valet parking.

restaurant.name: Navaratna
restaurant.area: 1 GST Rd, Le Royal Meridien, St. Thomas Mount
